skillRating.reasoning: This is a straightforward midrange deck with a linear game plan: curve out Kaneki variants, establish the energy line with Hinami, then deploy top-end threats like Yoshimura. The redundancy in the Kaneki package and character-dense build mean many turns play out similarly with limited branching decisions. While sequencing the energy line and timing when to commit resources matters moderately, the deck lacks disruption tools and interactive decision points that would force constant re-evaluation against different matchups. Mistakes in resource management or overextending into tempo decks are punished, but the deck's inherent engine does much of the heavy lifting once assembled.

strengths: Deep redundancy across four separate Iori Samura printings (006, 004, 005, base) lets the deck reliably flood its front line by turn two even on the draw.
Yoji Uruha copies (base and 018) provide early energy-line bodies that help the deck meet Chihiro Rokuhira's energy thresholds on curve.
The low overall AP cost of the Iori Samura swarm plays efficiently into Player One's 1/2/3 and Player Two's 2/2/3 AP ramp, letting the deck commit multiple bodies turn one-to-two.

Event support like 'Iai White Purity Style' and 'I Want to Protect My School Life' at 4 copies each suggests a repeatable combat trick or board-development tool that reinforces the aggressive swarm plan.
Chihiro Rokuhira's four distinct numbered variants (012, 013, 014, 015) give the deck a mid-game scaling threat once the Iori swarm has established board presence.
weaknesses: A 4.8 average placement against only one top-4 finish suggests the deck wins big when its swarm goes uncontested but collapses once an opponent stabilizes the board.
The synthesized list shows no clear removal, Snipe, or retire effects, so the deck cannot proactively clear blockers against higher-BP midrange decks like Solo Leveling - Sung Jinwoo.
With recency-weighted representation under 1% of the field, the deck has effectively been solved or out-paced by Tier 1 aggro like CSM - Denji and REZ - Rem, which likely out-race the Iori swarm.
Trigger composition is opaque in the data but the deck's poor resilience score implies a shallow Final/Active trigger suite, leaving it vulnerable once life cards start flipping under pressure.

The single-color mono-Kagurabachi build offers little flexibility to pivot into a defensive posture when the swarm plan is answered by board-wipe-adjacent tempo decks like Evangelion - Evangelion Test Type-01 Pseudo DMS Phase.

Heavy reliance on multiple numbered copies of the same named characters (Iori Samura x4 variants, Chihiro Rokuhira x4 variants) suggests redundancy without a clear top-end finisher to close games decisively.

The 0.6% recency-weighted meta share and 5.8 average placement indicate the deck currently struggles to convert its strengths into consistent top finishes against the modern field.
Without visible Damage(2) or Double Attack keywords in the listed cards, the deck likely needs multiple attack phases to close games, giving faster decks time to race it down.
Heavy reliance on recurring character plays (Tanaka, Kashima, Mad Horiguchi) suggests a front-line that can be ground down by Snipe or BP-battle-favored decks like Solo Leveling - Sung Jinwoo.

Overlapping color/archetype space with CSM - Denji (Tier 1) and CSM - Makima (Tier 2 control) means the deck is frequently outclassed in direct mirror-style matchups within its own IP.

main.name: I've Been Leveling Up This Whole Time

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: This midrange-tempo deck sits in the middle of the difficulty spectrum. While the Jinwoo/Jinah synergy engine and redundancy create a relatively forgiving core (high autopilot factor), the deck demands careful sequencing of resource recovery events, positioning decisions across multiple similar-costed characters, and timing of when to pivot from grinding to closing. The lack of disruption and proactive answers forces the pilot to read matchups and adapt their game plan mid-game, but the absence of tournament data and clear weaknesses against Tier 1 strategies suggest the deck doesn't punish mistakes as harshly as higher-tier lists—it simply loses to superior game plans rather than individual misplays.

strengths: Deep redundancy across Sung Jinwoo (015/016/017/020/021) gives the deck multiple copies of its core payoff, meaning a missing key piece is rarely fatal to the game plan.
Han Song-yi (002/003) as cheap early plays lets the energy line develop smoothly into the colors needed for Sung Jinwoo's thresholds by turn 2-3.
Arise and Mutilation at 4 copies each suggest a strong recurring trigger/board-impact engine that compounds as the game goes long.
Demon's Castle as a site likely provides passive energy or ability support without taking a front-line slot, freeing character slots for attackers.
Cha Hae-in (011) at 4 copies adds a secondary beater that diversifies the board beyond the Sung Jinwoo package, reducing single-point-of-failure risk.
weaknesses: No visible Snipe or hard removal means the deck cannot proactively answer an opponent's key threat, leaving it reactive against disruption-heavy builds like CSM - Makima.

The reliance on multiple named variants of the same character (Sung Jinwoo x5 different numbers) suggests a narrow, telegraphed game plan that experienced opponents can play around once the pattern is clear.
Against fast Tier 1 aggro such as REZ - Rem or CSM - Denji, the mid-game payoff orientation risks falling behind on life cards before Arise/Mutilation triggers can stabilize the board.
Zero recent tournament results indicate the deck has not proven itself against the current Tier 1/2 field, so its real-world matchup spread is largely untested and could be worse than projected.
Limited apparent flexibility means a poor opening hand missing early Han Song-yi copies can stall energy development, delaying the whole Sung Jinwoo curve.
